items.author: Poojan Patel
items.text: Poojan, the byte-level read is the right instrument. Same shape here: one record deleted from five agent memory stores, compaction run, files grepped. Two of five still held the bytes, both documented behaviour (a history log; a write-ahead log that keeps text until 1,020 more writes). A second record nobody deleted, kept as a control, saved us from one false positive. Does Tombstone keep a control marker per store?
items.why: Tombstone author (our article credits him); 7 reactions, 3 d; T5 concede then sharpen; target = profile until the post permalink is copied

items.author: Yaroslav Goncharov
items.text: The vector store row deserves a harder test than a stale-results window. We deleted one record from five agent memory stores, ran each compaction, then read the raw files: two of five still held the bytes, and all five delete calls had returned success. The test that catches it is a grep of the file, with an undeleted twin as the control. Which of your nine places gets a byte-level read rather than a query?
items.why: qatronic article on erasure reaching every system, cites EDPB 764 controllers; T1 missing piece; permalink pending

items.author: Hamza Shabbir
items.text: Memory trust verified rather than assumed is the right tier-three line, and the concrete version is cheap: after a delete, read the store's files, not its API. On five agent memory stores, one record deleted and compaction run, two of five still held the bytes; all five had returned success. That gap between a return code and the disk is where the poisoned-memory case lives too. Which layer owns that read, platform or security?
items.why: Principal AI architect, series on agent security tiers, 'memory trust verified rather than assumed'; T7 sharper question; permalink pending

items.author: Shreyas Gupta
items.text: The fourth problem hides inside the second: forgetting. Long-term memory has a delete call, and the call returning is not the same observable as the fact leaving the disk. On five agent memory stores, one record deleted and compaction run, two still held the bytes, both by documented design (a history log, a write-ahead log). Store conclusions, not transcripts, holds. Which of your three memories has a tested delete?
items.why: three kinds of agent memory, names Mem0/Zep/Letta, 2 h old; T1 missing piece (forgetting); permalink pending

items.author: Dr. Christabel Odeta
items.text: Q3 needs one more line. A soft delete with a tombstone leaves the bytes where they were, and a proof generated by the system that did the deleting is self-attestation. Measured: one record deleted from five agent memory stores, compaction run, raw files read. Two of five still held the bytes; all five delete calls returned success. The exercise I would add: grep the file after the worker finishes, with an undeleted twin as the control.
items.why: teaching post whose Q3 is a GDPR erasure design with soft delete plus proof; T5; permalink pending
